Rescue
res'kū
v.t. and n. (to deliver by force from danger or captivity; used of David recovering the captives, of a people saving Jonathan, and of God whom none can resist)
Old French rescourre, from Latin re and excutere, to shake out. Rescue implies force: it is not persuasion or ransom but taking back by strength what an enemy holds.

Biblical Definition

David at Ziklag is the pattern: “And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives” (1 Samuel 30:18). The whole company was taken and the whole company was brought back. The word also describes a congregation overruling its king: when Saul had sworn Jonathan must die for tasting honey, “the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid… So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not” (1 Samuel 14:45). David prays for it in a psalm: “Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions” (Psalm 35:17). And the most sobering use inverts it — when God is the one taking away, no rescue exists: “I will be unto Ephraim as a lion… I will take away, and none shall rescue him” (Hosea 5:14). The covenant curse of Deuteronomy says the same of a people under judgment: “thy sheep shall be given unto thine enemies, and thou shalt have none to rescue them” (Deuteronomy 28:31). Rescue is always by a stronger hand, and against the strongest there is none.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rescue as to free or deliver from confinement, violence, danger or evil, and notes it implies force or open violence.

expand to see more

RESCUE, v.t. To free or deliver from confinement, violence, danger or evil.

2. To retake; to take from an enemy by force.

RESCUE, n. The act of rescuing; deliverance from restraint, violence or danger; liberation from actual force.

RECOVER, v.t. To regain; to get or obtain that which was lost.

DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 30:18 — "And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives."

Psalm 35:17 — "Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions."

1 Samuel 14:45 — "And the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not."

Hosea 5:14 — "For I will be unto Ephraim as a lion, and as a young lion to the house of Judah: I, even I, will tear and go away; I will take away, and none shall rescue him."

Modern Corruption

Salvation is described as an offer of assistance to people in difficulty, and the biblical word means taking captives back by force.

expand to see more

Rescue implies three things the modern gospel presentation often omits: a real captor, real captives who cannot free themselves, and a rescuer strong enough to take them back. David did not negotiate with the Amalekites; he pursued and recovered. Where salvation is preached as an offer of help to people who are merely struggling, the doctrine of total depravity has gone quietly missing, and with it the necessity of a monergistic deliverance. Scripture's picture is of men taken captive by the devil at his will, delivered from the power of darkness and translated into the kingdom of God's dear Son. That is a rescue, and the rescued contribute nothing to it but their captivity.

Hosea 5:14 supplies the warning that the word cuts both ways. When God Himself is the lion, none shall rescue. There is no higher court, no stronger arm, no appeal. The comfort of Romans 8 — who shall separate us from the love of Christ — rests on the same fact from the other side: the hand that holds the believer is the hand nothing can pry open. The doctrine of God's omnipotence is a terror to His enemies and the only real security His people have, and both follow from the same sentence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew natsal, to snatch away, deliver — Psalm 35:17, Hosea 5:14, Deuteronomy 28:31; padah, to ransom — 1 Samuel 14:45; Greek exaireo (G1807), to take out — Acts 23:27, Galatians 1:4.

expand to see more

Hebrew natsal — to strip, snatch away, deliver; the common word behind rescue and deliver.

Hebrew padah — to ransom, to redeem by payment; 1 Samuel 14:45, of the people redeeming Jonathan.

Greek exaireo (G1807) — to take out, to rescue; Acts 23:27 of Paul taken from the mob, Galatians 1:4 of deliverance from this present evil world.

Greek ruomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to rescue; Colossians 1:13, delivered us from the power of darkness.

Colossians 1:13 gives the gospel in the vocabulary of rescue: delivered us from the power of darkness, and translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son.

Usage

"“David recovered all… and David rescued his two wives” — pursuit, not negotiation."

"“Rescue my soul from their destructions” — the prayer of a man who cannot free himself."

"“I will take away, and none shall rescue him” — against that hand there is no rescue."
